title: Every Filter Is a Delay: What Smoothing Costs the Loop

questions.question: A moving average over N samples reduces uncorrelated noise by how much, and costs what?
options: Noise falls as one over the square root of N, and it delays the signal by half the window
Noise falls as one over N, at no cost in delay
Noise falls as one over N, delaying by the whole window
Both scale with N, so the trade is neutral
questions.explanation: Both were measured against the theory in this lesson: 16 samples leaves 0.246 of the noise against a predicted 0.250, and lags by 7 samples against a predicted 7.5.

questions.question: Why divide by the number of readings held rather than by the window size?
options: Before the window is full they differ, and dividing by the window reports a fraction of the truth and climbs to it
It is faster
The window size may change
It avoids overflow
questions.explanation: At 500 Hz with a window of 64 that is an eighth of a second of a sensor reading low: short enough to miss in testing, long enough for a robot parked at a wall to start driving at it.

questions.question: A loop settling in 1.2 seconds is given filters of 64 and then 256 samples. What happens?
options: 64 settles in 1.18 s with 0.3 percent overshoot; 256 overshoots by 103 percent and never settles
Both are stable, the second merely slower
Both are unstable, the second more so
The second is smoother and therefore better
questions.explanation: The failure is not gradual. The filter that ruins it is the one whose lag is about a fifth of the settling time, because a delay in the feedback path is what destroys a loop.

questions.question: The same loop with no filter at all never settles either. Why?
options: The derivative term differentiates the noise, and a millimetre of jitter between samples two milliseconds apart is half a metre per second
The proportional gain is too high without smoothing
The integral term winds up on the noise
It settles, but outside the measured band
questions.explanation: Measured, it spends seven times the command effort and never settles. Too little filtering and too much are both unstable, and the window between them is wide but not infinite.

questions.question: Going from a window of 64 to 256 buys what, for what?
options: Another factor of two in noise, for four times the lag, which is why long filters are rarely worth it
A factor of four in noise for a factor of four in lag, a fair trade
Nothing at all
A factor of four in noise for twice the lag
questions.explanation: The noise reduction slows down as the square root while the lag grows linearly. That curve is the whole argument for keeping windows short.

questions.question: The noise needs more smoothing than the loop can afford in lag. What is the answer?
options: Not a longer average: a better trade for the same delay, a better sensor, or smoothing only what is displayed rather than what is fed back
Lengthen the filter and reduce the derivative gain to compensate
Lengthen the filter and accept the overshoot
Sample faster and keep the same window
questions.explanation: Sampling faster with the same window count does shorten the lag in seconds, and is worth knowing, but it does not change the trade between noise and delay at a given rate.
